section_summaries.epidemiology: Cryptococcosis, caused primarily by C. neoformans and C. gattii, is a major cause of mortality in AIDS patients, especially in sub-Saharan Africa. C. neoformans is cosmopolitan, while C. gattii is mostly found in tropical/sub-tropical areas but has spread to the Pacific Northwest. HIV infection is the primary risk factor, contributing to an estimated 225,000 cases of cryptococcal meningitis and over 135,000 deaths annually globally. HAART significantly reduces its incidence and associated mortality. Other risk factors in HIV-negative individuals include corticosteroid therapy, chronic lymphoid malignancies, solid organ transplantation, sarcoidosis, diabetes mellitus, and idiopathic CD4 lymphopenia. Males are more susceptible, and the disease is rare in children.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Disease with C. neoformans typically results from reactivation of a latent infection acquired by inhalation early in life, though acute pneumonia or primary skin infection can also occur. C. gattii disease onset is estimated 2-11 months post-exposure. Cryptococcus species are encapsulated yeasts, with glucuronoxylomannan in the capsule serving as a major virulence factor and diagnostic marker. Other virulence factors include growth at 37°C and melanin production. Invasion of the central nervous system (CNS) following fungemia leads to meningoencephalitis, where polysaccharide around pseudocysts contributes to brain edema and increased intracranial pressure. C. neoformans infection often shows a low inflammatory response, particularly in HIV-infected patients, unlike C. gattii, which can cause brain and lung granulomas. Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) is a granulomatous reaction occurring after HAART, distinguishable from cryptococcosis relapse.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Cryptococcus neoformans infections primarily manifest as meningoencephalitis in over 75% of cases, especially in HIV-infected patients, presenting with non-acute symptoms like dizziness, headache, nausea, and behavioral changes, often without meningeal irritation. Progressive infection can lead to vision/hearing impairment, coma, seizures, and palsies, with neurological abnormalities affecting up to 50% of patients. Lung disease is clinically non-distinctive, often presenting with low-grade fever, chest pain, and dry cough, with focal infiltrates being common. Disseminated infection can also involve the skin (≈5% of cases), presenting as ulcerated papules, and other sites such as blood (up to 45%), urine (15-30% in males), bones, joints, and lymph nodes. C. gattii infections should be considered in tropical areas and the Pacific Northwest, presenting with fever and cerebral/pulmonary masses that suggest malignancy, regardless of the patient's immune status.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis of cryptococcosis relies on identifying encapsulated yeasts, culture, and/or positive antigen detection in various body fluids. Patient evaluation includes cultures of CSF, urine, blood, sputum/bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and cryptococcal antigen testing in serum and CSF; larger fluid volumes increase diagnostic yield. India ink staining of fluid pellets or mucicarmine/alcian blue staining of tissue sections reveal encapsulated yeasts. Culture on Sabouraud agar at 30°C for up to 4 weeks (or longer with prior antifungal treatment) is standard, with lysis centrifugation improving blood detection. Commercial kits identify the genus via capsule presence, urease production, and assimilation patterns; molecular tools identify the species. Cryptococcal antigen detection in serum or CSF is highly effective for diagnosis in high-risk patients, with titers correlating with meningitis severity but varying based on host immune status, infection type, and kit. Screening AIDS patients before ART with pre-emptive fluconazole is associated with reduced meningitis incidence. Meningitis must be excluded in asymptomatic antigen-positive patients, as up to one-third may have it. Differential diagnosis is broad, as clinical features are non-distinctive and mimic lymphomas, other malignancies, or various opportunistic infections.
section_summaries.treatment: All patients with cryptococcal disease require treatment, despite case fatality rates still around 20% (higher in low-income regions). Treatment guidelines consider host immune status and clinical presentation. Severe cryptococcosis (meningoencephalitis, disseminated infection, acute pneumonia) involves an induction phase with amphotericin B (0.7-1.0 mg/kg/day) and flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day) for 2 weeks, with lipid formulations used for renal dysfunction and flucytosine levels monitored. In sub-Saharan Africa for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, initial treatment is 1 week of amphotericin B and flucytosine, followed by 1 week of high-dose fluconazole, or 2 weeks of high-dose fluconazole and flucytosine if amphotericin B is unavailable. Consolidation therapy with fluconazole (400-800 mg/day) is recommended for an additional 8 weeks. Corticosteroids are not recommended as adjuvant therapy. Maintenance therapy with fluconazole (200 mg/day) is given to AIDS patients until immune reconstitution occurs (CD4+ >100-200 cells/µL and undetectable viral load for >3 months post-ART). Milder forms are treated with fluconazole (400 mg/day) for 6-10 weeks. Control of elevated intracranial pressure is crucial, often requiring daily lumbar punctures to remove CSF if pressure is ≥25 cm H₂O, which is associated with ~70% survival. CSF shunting may be necessary if lumbar punctures fail. ART should be delayed for at least 2 weeks (or 4 weeks in meningitis) after cryptococcal disease treatment to prevent IRIS, which may be managed with short-course corticosteroids. Surgical excision is performed for pulmonary mass lesions caused by C. gattii.
section_summaries.prevention: Pre-emptive antifungal therapy with fluconazole is recommended for neurologically asymptomatic, HIV-infected patients with cryptococcal antigen positivity and CD4 counts <100 cells/mm³. This strategy, combined with antiretroviral therapy (ART), has significantly reduced mortality in advanced HIV-infected individuals.
